title: Raksha Bandhan (the thread)
hook: a plate with a lamp, red powder, rice, a sweet and a thread; the order you use them in is the ritual

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maha Shivaratri's pillar of light: a swan, a boar, a lying flower, and the one who said I couldn't find the end. Your line was no flower, no bluff.

On the full-moon morning of the month of Shravan, in the monsoon, a sister sets down a small steel plate. On it: a little oil lamp, a pinch of red powder, a few grains of rice, one sweet, and a thread. Sometimes a plain red-and-gold string, sometimes a plastic cartoon character her little brother will insist on wearing to school. Her brother sits facing her. Nobody needs instructions. They've done this every year since they were small. But there's an order to it, and the order is the whole ritual.
screen: `A STEEL PLATE, FIVE THINGS.` → `A SISTER, A BROTHER.` → `THE ORDER IS THE RITUAL.`

segments.voice: Here's how it goes in many homes. First the lamp is lit, and the sister circles it before her brother's face, a small arti. Then the tilak: red powder on his forehead, with a few grains of rice pressed into it. Then the thread, tied on his right wrist, with a knot or three. Then the sweet, placed in his mouth. Then his turn: a gift, and a promise to protect her. Raksha, protection. Bandhan, a bond. On days eighty-four and ninety-one you heard where the thread's stories come from: Draupadi tearing her sari to bind Krishna's cut finger, and Indra's wife tying a thread on him before battle. Today, look at the full moon itself, because the rakhi isn't the only thing tied on it. In many South Indian families, men who wear the sacred thread across the chest change it for a new one that morning, a day called Avani Avittam. On the coast of Maharashtra, fishing families offer coconuts to the sea, asking it to be gentle for the season. So Raksha Bandhan isn't really one custom. It's a full moon when people tie things: to each other, to the sea, to their own promises. And today, many sisters tie rakhis on sisters, cousins on cousins, friends on friends, and some people tie one on a tree they've promised to look after. Protection turns out to run in every direction.
screen: `LAMP, TILAK, THREAD, SWEET, PROMISE.` · `RAKSHA, PROTECTION. BANDHAN, A BOND.` · `ONE FULL MOON, MANY THREADS.` · `PROTECTION RUNS EVERY DIRECTION.`

segments.voice: On days eighty-four and ninety-one you were the one tying. This time, someone ties one on you: picture a person who has looked out for you without being asked, setting down the plate. The little lamp circles once before your face, a touch of red on your forehead, a thread pulled snug on your wrist with one knot, a sweet. Stay there a few breaths, the one being protected, and if you'd like, thank them silently.
Raksha Bandhan. The bond of protection, tied on the full moon of Shravan with a lamp, a tilak, a thread and a sweet.
Your line: protection runs in every direction. Sometimes yours is the wrist that gets the thread. One hundred fifty days now.

howItsDone: On the full moon of Shravan, many Hindu sisters perform a small arti for their brothers, apply a tilak, tie a rakhi on the wrist and feed them a sweet, and brothers give a gift and a promise of protection; today rakhis are also tied between sisters, cousins and friends.

fork.setup: you're the sister. the lamp is lit and circled, and the red tilak is on your brother's forehead. what comes next?
fork.reveal: the thread, tied on his right wrist. then the sweet, and only then his gift and his promise. the order is the ritual.

original.note: Sanskrit: raksha, protection, and bandhana, a tie or bond.

trapdoor: what it means: a full moon for tying protection: lamp, tilak, thread, sweet and a promise, in more directions than one.

what a scholar hears: Shravan Purnima carries several observances at once: Raksha Bandhan, upakarma (Avani Avittam), when those who wear the sacred thread renew it, and Narali Purnima on the Konkan coast.

sources.ref: Bhavishya Purana, Uttara Parva (Indrani ties a raksha on Indra)
Raksha Bandhan observance; Avani Avittam (upakarma); Narali Purnima

notes: Indrani (Shachi) tying a raksha on Indra: Bhavishya Purana, Uttara Parva 137. Confirm the reference.
Order of the ritual (arti, tilak with akshat, rakhi on right wrist, sweet, gift and promise): common but varies by family. Confirm.

Avani Avittam/upakarma: renewal of the yajnopavita on Shravan Purnima (for Rig and Yajur Vedins), mainly among communities who wear it. Written as 'in many South Indian families, men who wear the sacred thread'. Confirm.
Narali Purnima coconut offering by coastal (Koli) communities in Maharashtra. Confirm.
Tying rakhis on trees (vriksha bandhan): a modern practice. Confirm.
